H.R. 186 would require the commemorative work already authorized by section 1(a) of Public Law 117-80 to be located within the Reserve, notwithstanding 40 U.S.C. 8908(c). The work is the Medal of Honor monument authorized for the National Medal of Honor Museum Foundation; it is not authorization for a museum building. Except for this location provision, the bill expressly retains chapter 89, the Commemorative Works Act. Its findings are Congress's stated findings, not independent platform assessments of national importance or anyone's character.
The dated definition describes the Reserve as the Mall's great cross-axis as depicted on the named June 24, 2003 map 869/86501B. The captured official map's title/date/legend support that documentary identity; no exact parcel, current boundary or approved design is inferred. The dated 8908(c) baseline generally prohibits new commemorative works or visitor centers in the Reserve. The bill creates the specified location exception and requirement, not a repeal of the whole baseline.
The 2021 authorization already permitted the Foundation's commemorative work on Federal land in DC and its environs, required Commemorative Works Act compliance and prohibited Federal funds for establishment expenses, making the Foundation responsible for contributions and those expenses. It also governs excess funds and authority expiration. The remaining dated chapter 89 framework includes consultation, site/design approvals, construction-permit and sufficient-funding conditions, maintenance provisions and qualified expiration/extension rules. These are preserved references and dated context, not findings that the sponsor has met every condition. The bill does not itself appropriate money, issue a permit, select a precise parcel or establish completed construction.

The exact May 21 H.R. 1329 choice is the whole amended text printed after the House Resolution 1300 call-up: the committee substitute as modified by Part B of House Report 119-653. It is not the earlier introduced bill or a selected museum-building provision. The rule authorizes that deemed text and a motion to recommit; the retained call-up, printed whole text, rejected recommittal, final passage question, roll 188 and failure disposition support a candidate exact-action binding. Canonical binding remains pending review/application.
The bill would remove the existing Reserve-location exception from 80t-5(d), leaving the existing general Commemorative Works Act nonapplication, and replace the site provision with the South Monument site bounded by the four printed street descriptions, subject to a Presidential alternative within 180 days after enactment of the subsection. The dated baseline already considered a South Monument site and used 14th Street Northwest; the proposed text prints Southwest. The candidate preserves those documentary descriptions without correcting one, mapping a parcel or finding a present site approval.
Administrative jurisdiction over the designated land would transfer to the Smithsonian as soon as practicable after enactment of the subsection. Planning, design and construction would remain may authority with consultation and approval by the listed bodies and agency/entity head. The new criteria include qualified protection of open space/public use/cultural and natural resources, durable outdoor materials, climate-compatible landscaping and mutually agreed site-specific guidelines. The Smithsonian would reimburse the agency/entity head within the printed 60 day period for costs incurred implementing recommendations from that approval process; the candidate does not invent an unstated trigger for that period. The baseline's 50 percent Federal/50 percent non-Federal cost-sharing and open authorization are not a new bill appropriation or proof of available construction funding.
The whole choice would also add the bill's stated mission concerning the history, achievements and lived experiences of biological women in the United States and its prohibition on depicting a biological male as female. These are attributed proposed statutory terms, not platform identity classifications or inferred member motives. The dated Council baseline already requires, to the extent practicable, equal representation of diverse political viewpoints. The bill replaces that clause and adds authentic-experience and defined guidance-source requirements. Council exhibits/programs would reflect, to the extent practicable, equal representation of a range of political viewpoints and authentic experiences; the Council would seek and use guidance from the defined broad array of knowledgeable/respected sources for creation and substantial revision. This is not a party quota or a finding that existing exhibits violate a rule.
A report would be due within 120 days after enactment and every two years thereafter to the seven named committees, addressing the actions described by the bill. The report clause literally refers to amendments made by subsection (f) inside subsection (f); no intended replacement is supplied. The section and amendments would take effect as if included in title I of division T of the 2021 Act. Those are the bill's proposed retroactive-effective words, not a conclusion that the failed House choice took effect. Roll 188 failed; neither enactment, construction, a current mission change nor present administrative compliance is inferred.

The whole exact choice is Hunt Part A amendment 7 to H.R. 8800, not the neighboring Part A 6 certification offering or Part A 8 refinery study and not whole-bill passage. The printed own offering, its question/postponement, resumed designation of the same amendment, roll 260 and agreement disposition support a candidate exact-action binding. The rule binds the amendment process to the identified bill. These sources do not turn the House agreement into enacted land acquisition, a license, an operating project or a national-security finding by the platform.
The Secretary of Defense would be authorized to acquire permanent easements by purchase, donation, exchange or condemnation along the named Santa Ynez Pipeline System, including State-held lands, as the Secretary determines necessary for specified crude-oil transport to domestic refineries supplying Defense installations in California. The named Gaviota, State-submerged and additional-route easements retain their purposes/necessity qualifications. The object is an easement, not fee title to every California parcel.
Condemnation may proceed in the district where the property is located, citing 10 U.S.C. 2663 and the printed subchapter III of 40 U.S.C.chapter 31. The dated Code labels III as Bonds and places the separately cited 3114 taking provision in II, Acquiring Land. The printed III is visually confirmed and retained without inferred correction or legal-validity outcome. The proposal states Congress's vital-national-security/delay findings and permits commencement before the otherwise required report, with a report within seven days after commencement. Dated 2663 already has a qualified advanced-report exception and seven-day reporting; the candidate does not present that idea as wholly new or infer an actual Secretary determination.
California could not assert the printed sovereign-immunity/title/State-law defenses to these condemnation proceedings. Immediate possession/use would follow BOTH a 3114 declaration of taking and deposit of estimated just compensation; a court could not condition it on the specified State approvals. Proceedings would receive docket priority and expedited resolution. Compensation payable to California or its agencies would be determined in the district court, or the Court of Federal Claims if the parties elect, accounting for the named retained Federal powers for submerged-land easements. An estimated deposit is not final compensation, and this does not determine present title, jurisdiction or a constitutional outcome.
Upon acquisition, Defense would issue the system operator a license for the specified easement use and Defense-supply purpose, with terms requiring applicable Federal chapter 601 pipeline safety compliance. Revocation/suspension/modification/termination exceptions are alternatives: an Act of Congress expressly referencing this section by name and subsection, OR a Defense Secretary path after a final Transportation order (or a sustaining final court-of-appeals judgment if challenged), an imminent public-safety hazard and failure to cure within a reasonable period after written notice/opportunity. State-court determinations and other executive/administrative actions have distinct no-revocation clauses. The license is not absolutely exceptionless or terminable for any alleged violation.
Transfer to a successor operator would require chapter 601 compliance; holding the required authorizations is deemed compliance only for that transfer paragraph. During an issued license, the continuity paragraph removes State/local authorizations only to the extent obtaining or maintaining them would in practice halt or substantially delay the licensed easement use, and that paragraph expressly preserves Federal law/permits/agency authority. Separately, subsection (e)(2)has broader California authorization/lease/permit/approval wording for operation, maintenance, repair or use of any system segment. These scopes are not flattened into a single test or a repeal of every Federal requirement.
The other State-law preemption branch covers preventing/conditioning/delaying Defense authority OR preventing operator use of acquired easements; the operator-use branch does not borrow the other branch's verbs. The litigation clause concerns State relief in proceedings to which the United States is not a party. Subsection(f)asserts the proposed retained-Federal-power/State-title priority rule for the named submerged lands; it is not the platform's adjudication of title. The dated 1314 baseline expressly distinguishes paramount Federal powers from proprietary ownership and retains its due-process/just-compensation language. No actual conflict or litigation outcome is decided.
Defense may require reimbursement of all or part of acquisition costs, including compensation paid to a State or private party, credited to the original account; full reimbursement and a new stated appropriation are not mandated. All five printed geographic/system definitions remain: approximately four-mile Gaviota segment; the specified Las Flores CA-324/325 network with former 901/903 labels; the complete named offshore/onshore Santa Ynez network; its defined Federal offshore production unit; and State-submerged lands under the named Act. Selected dated OCSLA/pipeline-safety definitions, State/Federal limits, hazardous-facility orders and judicial review are context, not actual facility classification, exhaustive current regulations, safety certification, current operator/lease status or a general finding that the project is needed or authorized today.

H.R.859 would require the manufacturer of a covered device to disclose clearly and conspicuously, before purchase, whether the device contains a camera or microphone as a component. Its covered-device definition uses the printed consumer-product reference to section3(a) of the Consumer Product Safety Act and requires internet capability and a camera or microphone. It excludes telephones including mobile phones, laptops, tablets and devices a consumer would reasonably expect to have a camera or microphone; devices specifically marketed as a camera, telecommunications device or microphone; and devices or apparatus described in the named Communications Act provisions (47U.S.C.255,617,619and303(aa)/(bb)) and associated regulations. These are the bill's categories and literal incorporations, not classifications of actual products.

A section2 violation would receive the bill's specified unfair-or-deceptive-rule treatment. The FTC would enforce the Act through the incorporated applicable FTC Act terms, with the stated penalties, privileges and immunities and a savings clause for its other authority. No particular penalty amount or additional unstated enforcement power is asserted.

Within180days after enactment, the FTC would issue guidance through outreach to relevant private entities. The guidance would address clear, conspicuous and age-appropriate disclosure as practicable, and best practices for pictorial representation. The referenced definition uses includes for pictures, photographs, video, illustrations and symbols; the bill does not independently require a particular icon. Manufacturers could petition for tailored guidance consistent with existing or successor rules of practice. Guidance would not confer rights on any person, State or locality, or bind the FTC or any person. An enforcement action must allege a specific statutory violation; inconsistency with guidance alone is insufficient unless the practices allegedly violate section2.

The bill would apply to covered devices manufactured after the date180days after the FTC issues section3(c) guidance. It would not apply to devices manufactured or sold before that date, or otherwise introduced into interstate commerce before it. The enactment-relative guidance deadline and the guidance-relative applicability date are distinct; no clock is found to have started from House passage.

The five dated statutory context readings explain the pictorial reference and named accessibility frameworks while preserving their printed conditions and reference notes. They do not add those baseline accessibility duties to H.R.859. Incorporated regulations and category definitions remain literal references; this candidate does not determine exhaustive current regulatory coverage, classify an actual device or certify current law.

H.R.152 would replace section1223 of the Disaster Recovery Reform Act of2018. Within two years after enactment of the section, the Administrator, coordinating with the named agencies, would study and plan improvements to disaster-applicant and grantee information collection and plan regular federal disaster-assistance reporting, including a public website. A regularly convened interagency working group would identify duplication in preliminary damage assessments, assess a single-agency approach and identify potential emerging technologies such as unmanned aircraft systems, consistent with the named2017 FEMA systems requirements.
The Administrator would submit one comprehensive report containing the plans and working-group findings, which may include recommendations, to the two named congressional committees. FEMA would publish pre-compressed easily downloadable versions in appropriate formats and machine-readable form if applicable. Available publications, databases and other information could be used. A requested briefing would be due within180days after report submission.
The dated2018 section being replaced required a study and plans within one year after its enactment; it did not contain this entire new working-group/report scheme. The separate2017 law concerns grant-system modernization with its own qualifications. This bill does not order deployment of drones or implementation of every recommendation. House passage starts no enactment-relative clock.

H.R.153 would require OMB, consulting Treasury and covered agencies, to establish a subpage within the FFATA website for the bill's disaster-assistance information. Within30days after each calendar quarter, a covered agency that made assistance available to an eligible recipient would publish quarterly totals, expended or obligated amounts and a detailed project/activity list with the specified identifiers, location, completion status and collected reporting information, and ensure agency data assets are machine readable. Agencies would issue necessary guidance; OMB could use a private-entity agreement if necessary for transparency.
Covered agencies are Stafford-assistance agencies, SBA and HUD. The bill defines disaster assistance as federal funds responding to a specified natural disaster, including the enumerated SBA, HUD and Stafford forms. Eligible recipients are direct federal recipient entities, including States, other than individuals; a grant, loan or contract can qualify. Its four-part natural-disaster definition is retained. These printed references describe the reporting scope without certifying every incorporated program's current rules or a particular recipient's eligibility.
The existing dated FFATA section already supplied public award reporting and machine-readable/open-data requirements with its own historical dates, thresholds and exceptions. The proposed subpage, quarterly disaster fields and bill-specific definitions are the exact change. Its reporting scope does not inherit an unstated $25,000 threshold from that baseline. It does not itself award disaster funding or build the projects being reported.

H.R.164 would add subsection(e) to Stafford Act section403. An electric utility could carry out cost-effective hazard mitigation jointly or otherwise in combination with power-restoration activities receiving section403 assistance. Receipt of section403 emergency power-restoration assistance would not render a facility ineligible for section406 hazard mitigation assistance for which it is otherwise eligible. The amendment would apply only to amounts appropriated on or after enactment.
The dated403 baseline provides essential assistance under its own conditions; the dated406 baseline covers qualifying public and private nonprofit facilities and preserves eligibility, cost-share and other restrictions. The definitions provide context for public and private nonprofit facilities, rather than proving that every utility qualifies. This bill changes the coordination and non-disqualification rules, not every baseline condition.
It does not appropriate a specified amount, guarantee funding, erase cost-effectiveness or otherwise-eligible limits, or make all electric utilities eligible. House passage alone does not establish enactment or applicability to an actual appropriation.
